title: What is space? Near, far, and whether space goes on for ever

summary.text: Walk away from a bottle, and it looks smaller, though the bottle stays the same. What changed is the space between you and the bottle. Space is the room around things and between them. The farther apart two things are, the more space is between them. Nobody knows yet whether space goes on for ever.
summary.art: A girl in a flat holding a pencil up at arm's length, one eye closed, measuring a water bottle on a stool across the room.

intro.hook: Hold up your thumb at arm's length and close one eye. Can your small thumb hide a big building far outside your window?
intro.text: A thumb is much smaller than a building. Yet if the building is far enough away, your thumb can hide it. In this unit you find out why. You hunt for spaces in your home and count steps to near and far things. You measure how big a bottle looks from far away. Then you make a tunnel of mirrors that seems to go on for ever, and ask whether space does.
intro.art: A child's hand held out with the thumb up, covering a tall building far across the roofs, and the child's one closed eye.

outcomes: By the end I can say that space is the room around things and between them, and find spaces in my home.
By the end I can use near, nearer, nearest, far, farther and farthest, and count steps to compare distances.
By the end I can show that the same thing looks smaller when it is farther away.
By the end I can say why the Sun, the Moon and a plane in the sky look small, though they are big.
By the end I can say that nobody knows yet whether space goes on for ever, and say why it is hard to find out.
By the end I can say that the space in my room is full of air, while outer space is almost empty.

terms.meaning: Space is the room around things and between them. Everything is somewhere in space.
terms.example: There is space between your bed and the wall. There is space between the Earth and the Moon.
terms.art: A bed and a wall with a gap between them, and an arrow across the gap labelled 'space'.

terms.meaning: Distance is how much space there is between two things. We can measure it in steps, centimetres or kilometres.
terms.example: The distance from your bed to the door might be 5 steps.
terms.art: A child walking heel to toe from a bed to a door, with numbers 1 to 5 under her feet.

terms.meaning: Near means a small distance away. Far means a big distance away.
terms.example: Your pillow is near your head. The Moon is far from your bed.
terms.art: A child on a bed with a pillow beside her, and the Moon small in the window.

terms.meaning: Between means in the space that separates two things.
terms.example: In a row of chappals by the door, the middle chappal is between the other two.
terms.art: Three chappals in a row at a door, with the middle one circled.

terms.meaning: Outer space is the space above the Earth's air, where the Moon, the Sun and the stars are. It is almost empty.
terms.example: Rockets from Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh fly up through the air and into outer space.
terms.art: A rocket rising from a launch pad by the sea, with the blue sky fading to black above it.

terms.meaning: The universe is all of space and everything in it: every star, planet, rock, plant, animal and person.
terms.example: You, your home, the Earth, the Sun and all the stars are part of the universe.
terms.art: A child's house drawn small inside a big circle full of stars and swirls of galaxies.

terms.meaning: A reflection is the picture you see in a mirror or in still water. It is made by light bouncing off the shiny surface.
terms.example: You see your face as a reflection in the bathroom mirror, or in a steel plate.
terms.art: A girl looking at her face in a shiny steel plate.

terms.meaning: To estimate is to make a careful guess about a number, before you count or measure it.
terms.example: You estimate that the door is 6 steps away. Then you walk and count 5 steps.
terms.art: A child with a thought bubble showing '6?' next to a door.

explanations.concept: Space is what is between things
explanations.context: This card explains what space is, after your hunt for spaces in your home.
explanations.definition: Space is the room around things and between them. Everything is somewhere in space. Things can move because there is space to move into.
explanations.description: In the space hunt, you found space under your bed, between your fingers and inside an empty bottle. You can push two tumblers together, but there is still space all around them. Space is not only up in the sky. It is right here, between your nose and this page. Every thing takes up some space, and the space around it lets it move.
examples: The gap between your bed and the wall
The room inside an empty tiffin box
The space between the Earth and the Moon
explanations.art: A room seen from above, with bed, cupboard and mat, and the empty floor between them shaded lightly and labelled 'space'.

explanations.context: This card explains near and far, after you counted steps to things in your home.
explanations.definition: Distance is how much space there is between two things. Near means a small distance. Far means a big distance.
explanations.description: In Step It Out, the bed was fewer steps away than the door, so the bed was nearer. We use steps for short distances at home. For longer ones, we use metres and kilometres. A kilometre is about 1,300 steps of a grown-up. The Moon is about 384,000 kilometres away. That is so far that walking there, day and night without stopping, would take about 9 years.
examples: 3 steps to the bed, and 7 steps to the door
A short walk to the corner shop
The very long way to the Moon
explanations.art: A line from a child's toes to a door, a road to a shop, and a dotted path up to the Moon, each longer than the last.

explanations.context: This card explains what you found in the bottle strip test.
explanations.definition: A thing looks smaller when it is farther away, because it takes up less of what your eyes can see. From twice as far away, it looks about half as tall.
explanations.description: In the bottle strip test, the bottle never changed. But from 2 steps away it looked about half as tall as from 1 step. From 4 steps, it looked about a quarter as tall. That is why a big plane high in the sky looks as small as a bird. The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon. It is also about 400 times farther away. So in the sky, the two look about the same size.
examples: A plane high up looking as small as a bird
A tall gopuram that your thumb can hide from far away
The Sun and the Moon looking the same size
explanations.art: Three identical bottles in a row going away from a child's eye, with the paper strips beside them getting shorter.

explanations.context: This card explains what is in space, in your room and far above the Earth.
explanations.definition: The space in your room is full of air, though you cannot see it. Outer space, between the stars, is almost empty.
explanations.description: The space between your bed and the wall looks empty. But it is full of air, made of tiny bits far too small to see. Wave your hand fast, and you feel them. High above the Earth, the air gets thinner and thinner. Out between the stars, a space the size of a sugar cube holds about one tiny bit of gas, or even less. Yet light from the Sun and stars crosses that space all the time.
examples: Air you feel when you wave your hand
Thin air on a high mountain in Ladakh
Almost empty space between the stars
explanations.art: A sugar cube shape drawn twice: one crowded with dots labelled 'air in your room', one with a single dot labelled 'space between the stars'.

explanations.concept: Does space go on for ever?
explanations.context: This card is about a question nobody can answer yet. You thought about it with the mirror tunnel.
explanations.description: Nobody knows. We can only see part of space. Light from very far away has not had time to reach us yet, so we cannot see what is beyond. In the mirror tunnel, you could not see the end of the row either. The copies got too small and dim. Not seeing an end does not tell us whether there is one. Scientists measure the shape of space to find clues, and they still disagree.
examples: The mirror tunnel, where the end was too small and dim to see
Looking at the night sky and seeing only the nearest stars
Asking 'and what is past that?' again and again

perspectives.explanation: Space may go on for ever, with no end at all. Measurements of space so far fit this idea.
Space may be very, very big but not endless. It could curve round on itself, like the skin of a ball, which has no edge but is not endless.

perspectives.who: Archytas, a thinker in ancient Greece, about 2,400 years ago
perspectives.explanation: If space had an edge, you could stand there and push a stick out. Either the stick goes on, so there is more space, or something stops it, so there is something beyond. So space has no edge.

explanations.art: A child standing at a pretend wall at the edge of the stars, pushing a stick through it, with a question mark beyond.

agreed.text: Everything is somewhere in space, and there is space between all things.
agreed.evidence: In the space hunt, every thing you looked at had space around it, even two tumblers pushed together.

agreed.text: The same thing looks smaller when it is farther away.
agreed.evidence: In the bottle strip test, the bottle looked about half as tall from twice as far, and the bottle did not change.

agreed.text: The Sun is much bigger than the Moon and much farther away.
agreed.evidence: Astronomers have measured both. The Sun is about 400 times wider and about 400 times farther away. That is why they look the same size.
Spacecraft have measured it. Between the stars, there is only about one tiny bit of gas in a space the size of a sugar cube.

challenging.claim: The sky is a roof over the Earth, with the stars stuck on it, all the same distance away.
challenging.who: Many people long ago, in many countries, including the Greek thinker Aristotle.
challenging.for: The stars all look equally far away. They all turn across the night sky together, as if stuck on one roof.
challenging.against: In 1838, Friedrich Bessel measured how far away one star was. Since then, astronomers have measured many stars. They are at very different distances. Rockets fly up through the sky and find no roof.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of what the sky is.

challenging.claim: Things far away really are smaller, and they grow as you walk nearer.
challenging.who: Many young children think this at first.
challenging.for: From far away, a bus or a person really does look small.
challenging.against: In the bottle strip test, the bottle looked smaller from far away, but you could walk back and pick up the same bottle. Only the distance changed.
challenging.context: This card is about a mistake many of us make at first.

challenging.claim: Space is a thing of its own, like a huge empty box. It would still be there even with nothing in it.
challenging.who: Isaac Newton, an English scientist, about 340 years ago. Gottfried Leibniz, a German thinker, disagreed. He said space is only how things sit apart from each other.
challenging.for: Things move through space, and space seems to be there whether or not things fill it.
challenging.against: We only ever measure space by the distances between things. With no things at all, nobody could tell if there was any space.
challenging.context: This card is about a question thinkers still argue about: is space something, or only the gaps between things?

big_questions.q: If you took every single thing out of a room, even the air, would there still be space in the room?
big_questions.hint: Think of the space hunt. Was the space the things, or the room around them?

big_questions.q: Your thumb can hide a building. How can you tell whether a thing is small, or big and far away?
big_questions.hint: Think of the bottle strip test. What did you need to know besides how big the bottle looked?

big_questions.q: If space has an edge, what is on the other side of it?
big_questions.hint: Think of Archytas pushing a stick through the edge of space.

big_questions.q: The stars look tiny. If you could fly to one, how big would it look?
big_questions.hint: The Sun is a star. It is the nearest one to us.

big_questions.q: A crow sitting on a wire keeps a gap between her and the next crow. Why might birds need space around them?
big_questions.hint: Watch birds on a wire or a ledge. Do they sit touching, or apart?

how_we_found_out.story: A hundred years ago, many astronomers thought our Milky Way was the whole of space. The Milky Way is our home group of stars, called a galaxy. In the sky they could see faint, misty patches. Many thought these were small clouds inside the Milky Way. To find out, they needed to know how far away the patches were. Henrietta Swan Leavitt made that possible. She worked at Harvard College Observatory in the United States, studying photographs of stars, for very little pay. She studied stars that get brighter and dimmer, again and again, over days. In 1912 she showed that the slower such a star changes, the brighter it really is. If you know how bright a star really is, and see how bright it looks, you can work out how far away it is. In 1923, Edwin Hubble found one of these stars in the misty patch called Andromeda. Using Leavitt's rule, he showed that Andromeda is far outside the Milky Way. It is a whole galaxy of its own, and space is far bigger than people had thought.
how_we_found_out.who: Henrietta Swan Leavitt, an American astronomer at Harvard College Observatory. Edwin Hubble, an American astronomer at Mount Wilson Observatory.
how_we_found_out.when: Leavitt's rule in 1912. Hubble found the star in Andromeda in 1923 and announced his result in 1925.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the Milky Way was the whole of space, and the misty patches were small clouds inside it. Leavitt's way of measuring distance showed that Andromeda is a separate galaxy, very far away.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman at a desk by a window, looking through a magnifying glass at a glass photograph covered in dots of stars.

story.title: Nila and the Wall at the End of the Sky
story.note: Nila, Adi and their Paati are made up. Paati means grandmother in Tamil. Archytas was a real thinker in ancient Greece.
text: Nila was eight. She lived in a flat on the fourth floor in Madurai, with her Paati and her little brother Adi. Adi was five.
One evening the power went off. The fan stopped, and the flat went dark and warm. Paati lit a lamp, and they all went out to sit on the balcony.
From the balcony, they could see the tall gopuram of the Meenakshi temple, far across the roofs. Its top was lit up by the last of the sunset.
Adi held up his thumb and closed one eye. "Look, Akka," he said. "I can hide the whole gopuram with my thumb!"
Nila laughed. "Your thumb is not bigger than the gopuram," she said. "The gopuram is just very far away. Things look smaller when they are far."
Adi looked at his thumb, then at the gopuram. He moved his thumb away, and the gopuram came back. He put his thumb back, and it was gone again. He did this six times.
Then the stars began to come out, one by one. Adi lay back on the mat and looked up.
"Akka," he said, "where does the sky stop? Is there a wall at the end?"
Nila thought about it. "Let's play a game," she said. "I'll say a place, and you say what is past it."
"Past our balcony?" she asked. "The street," said Adi. "Past the street?" "The temple." "Past the temple?" Adi thought hard. "More roofs. Then the hills."
"Past the hills?" "The sea, I think." "Past the sea, and up, up into the sky?" "The Moon!" said Adi. "Past the Moon?" "The Sun. And then the stars."
"And past the very last star?" asked Nila.
Adi sat up. "A wall," he said. "A big wall at the end of the sky."
"All right," said Nila. "What is on the other side of the wall?"
Adi opened his mouth, then shut it. He frowned. "More space," he said slowly. "But then the wall is not the end."

Paati smiled in the lamplight. "A thinker in Greece asked that same question, about 2,400 years ago," she said. "His name was Archytas. He said: if I stood at the edge of space and pushed out a stick, where would the stick go? Either there is more space for it, or something is there to stop it. People are still thinking about his question."
"So does space go on for ever?" asked Adi.
"Nobody knows yet," said Paati. "Not me, and not the scientists either. That is one of the biggest questions there is."
Nila jumped up. "I can show you something that looks like for ever," she said. She went inside and came back with Paati's small hand mirror. She stuck a red bindi on the top edge of the mirror.
She took Adi to the big mirror on the cupboard door and held the hand mirror up in front of it, facing the big mirror. "Look over the top," she said.
Adi looked. He gasped. Inside the big mirror was the hand mirror. Inside that was another, and another, each one smaller, a long tunnel of mirrors going away. Each had a red bindi on top.
"It goes on for ever!" said Adi.
"Count them," said Nila.
Adi counted. "One, two, three" all the way to eleven. Then the bindis were too tiny and too dark to see.
"Is that the end?" he asked.
"I don't know," said Nila. "I can't see any more. But not seeing the end doesn't tell us if there is an end."
Just then the power came back. The fan began to turn, and the lights came on all over the street.
Adi went back to the balcony. He held up his thumb and hid the gopuram once more. Then he looked up at the stars. "They must be very, very far," he said, "to look so small."
story.epiphany: Far things look small because of the space between us and them, not because they are small. And when we ask what is past the farthest place, there always seems to be another question. Nobody knows yet whether space has an end.
ask: Adi hid the whole gopuram with his thumb. Was his thumb bigger than the gopuram? Why could it hide the gopuram?
When Nila asked what was on the other side of the wall, why did Adi say the wall was not the end?
In the mirror tunnel, Adi counted eleven bindis. Why could he not count any more?
Nila said that not seeing the end doesn't tell us if there is an end. What did she mean?
What do you think: does space go on for ever? What makes you think so?
art: A girl, a small boy and their grandmother on a balcony in Madurai at dusk, a lamp beside them and a temple gopuram far off over the roofs.
A small boy with one eye shut, holding up his thumb so it covers the distant gopuram.
The boy lying on a mat looking up at the first stars, with his sister beside him.
The grandmother in the lamplight, holding up a stick as she tells them about Archytas.
The boy looking over a hand mirror into a cupboard mirror, with a long tunnel of smaller and smaller mirrors, each with a red bindi.

experiments.title: The Bottle Strip Test: how big does a bottle look from far away?
experiments.context: In this experiment you measure how tall a bottle looks from 1 step, 2 steps and 4 steps away. You use a pencil held out at arm's length, the way artists measure. Then you compare the paper strips.
experiments.question: When you stand twice as far from a bottle, how tall does the bottle look?
experiments.predict: When you stand twice as far away, will the bottle look just as tall, a little shorter, or half as tall? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same bottle the whole time, and we never move it. The child holds the pencil the same way every time, with the arm straight and one eye closed, because a bent arm changes the size. Only the distance changes. We measure at each place twice, in case one try goes wrong.
results_table: How many 4-step strips fit along it

materials.item: a water bottle, half-litre size, or a tall steel tumbler
a stool, a chair or a low table to stand the bottle on
a long strip of paper, such as a sheet of notebook paper cut lengthwise
3 chappals or slips of paper to mark the places on the floor

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the cutting with scissors.

schedule.what: Measure the bottle with a pencil from 1, 2 and 4 steps away. Mark and cut the strips. Compare them.

experiments.record: Glue or lay the three strips side by side on a page, longest first. Write '1 step', '2 steps' and '4 steps' under them.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results, from Kavya's flat in Mysuru
cols: How many 4-step strips fit along it

setup.art: A water bottle standing on a stool at one end of a room, with three chappals on the floor at 1, 2 and 4 big steps away.
setup.caption: 1. Stand the bottle on a stool. Mark 1, 2 and 4 steps away.

setup.art: A child at the first chappal, arm held straight, one eye closed, a pencil upright with its tip at the top of the bottle and her thumbnail at the bottom.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the pencil out straight. Close one eye. Slide your thumb to the bottom of the bottle.

setup.art: The pencil laid on a paper strip, with a grown-up marking the paper at the pencil tip and at the thumb.
setup.caption: 3. Lay the pencil on the paper. Mark the tip and the thumb.

setup.art: Three strips of paper side by side, the second half as long as the first, the third half as long as the second.
setup.caption: 4. Cut the strips and lay them side by side.

flow.do: 1. Stand the bottle on a stool at one end of the longest room or hall. 2. From the bottle, take 1 big step and put a chappal down. 3. Take 1 more big step and put a second chappal. 4. Take 2 more big steps and put the third chappal.
flow.say: This chappal is 1 step from the bottle. This one is 2 steps. This one is 4 steps, twice as far as the second.
flow.kid: Look at the chappals. One is 1 step away. One is 2 steps. One is 4 steps.
flow.parent: Use your own big steps, and keep them all the same length. You need about 3 metres in a straight line. A hall, a corridor or the space from a bedroom door to the far wall works.
flow.context: This is the first step of the bottle strip test. You mark the places to stand.

flow.do: 1. Ask the questions below. 2. Write your child's guess and reason at the top of the paper. 3. Do not say who is right.
flow.say: From 2 steps, how tall will the bottle look? Now think of 4 steps, which is twice as far. Will it look just as tall, a little shorter, or half as tall? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: From twice as far, how tall will the bottle look? Why?

ask.q: From twice as far away, how tall will the bottle look? Why?
good: The same, because it is the same bottle.
A bit smaller, because far things look small.
Half, because it is twice as far.

flow.parent: Most children guess 'the same' or 'a bit smaller'. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: In this step of the bottle strip test, you make your guess.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands with toes at the 1-step chappal. 2. Arm straight out, elbow locked, one eye closed. 3. Hold the pencil upright. Line up the tip with the top of the bottle. 4. Slide the thumbnail down to the bottom of the bottle. 5. Keep the thumb still, and lay the pencil on the paper strip. 6. You mark the paper at the tip and at the thumb.
flow.say: Hold your arm out straight, like a stick. Close one eye. Put the pencil tip at the top of the bottle. Now slide your thumb down to the bottom. Keep it still, and we'll mark it.
flow.kid: Arm out straight. Close one eye. Tip at the top. Thumb at the bottom. Keep still.
flow.parent: The arm must be straight every time, or the measure changes. If your child finds it hard, you hold your own arm out and measure, and your child checks. Do each place twice. The two marks should be close.
flow.context: In this step of the bottle strip test, you measure the bottle from 1 step away.

flow.do: 1. Move to the 2-step chappal and measure the same way. 2. Mark a new piece of the strip. 3. Then measure from the 4-step chappal. 4. Mark a third piece. 5. Write '1', '2' and '4' next to the marks.
flow.say: Now we're twice as far. Measure again, with your arm just as straight. Now the last chappal, twice as far again.
flow.kid: Measure from 2 steps. Then measure from 4 steps.

ask.q: As you stepped back, what happened to the gap between your pencil tip and your thumb?
good: It got smaller.
My thumb went up nearer the tip.

flow.parent: From 4 steps the mark may be only 2 or 3 centimetres long. That is fine. Small is the result.
flow.context: In this step of the bottle strip test, you measure from 2 steps and 4 steps away.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the three marked pieces. 2. Lay them side by side, longest first. 3. Fold the 1-step strip in half and hold it next to the 2-step strip. 4. Count how many 4-step strips fit along the 1-step strip. 5. Fill in the results table. 6. Then read the cards on near and far.
flow.say: Let's fold the 1-step strip in half. Is half of it as long as the 2-step strip? How many little 4-step strips fit along the long one? Did the bottle change, or did something else change?
flow.kid: Fold the long strip in half. Is it like the middle strip? Did the bottle change?

ask.q: The bottle never moved. What changed?
good: How far away I stood.
The space between me and the bottle.
Only the distance.

check.q: In the bottle strip test, you stood twice as far from the bottle. How tall did the bottle look?
check.why: From twice as far away, the bottle takes up about half as much of what you see, so it looks about half as tall. The bottle did not shrink. Only the distance changed.

flow.parent: Usually the 2-step strip is close to half the 1-step strip, and about 3 to 5 of the 4-step strips fit along the 1-step one. Steps that are not quite even, or an arm that bends, make it less exact. A strong answer uses the strips as evidence: same bottle, more space between, shorter strip.
flow.context: This is the last step of the bottle strip test. You compare the strips and say what you found.

experiments.title: The Mirror Tunnel: does the row go on for ever?
experiments.context: In this experiment you hold a small mirror facing a big mirror. You see a tunnel of mirrors going away, each with a bindi on top. You count the bindis to find out whether the row goes on for ever.
experiments.question: In a tunnel of mirrors, how many copies can you count? Does the row go on for ever?
experiments.predict: How many bindis will you be able to count: 2, 10, 100, or never-ending? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Two people count, each three times, holding the mirror in the same place. We count three times because it is easy to lose your place in a long row.
results_table: What the last copies looked like

materials.item: a big mirror on a wall or a cupboard door
a bindi or a small sticker

experiments.safety: Glass mirrors break and cut. A grown-up carries the mirrors, and the child holds the hand mirror with both hands.

schedule.what: Make the mirror tunnel. Count the bindis three times each. Talk about whether the row goes on for ever.

experiments.record: Write each count in the results table. Draw the tunnel as you saw it, with the bindis getting smaller.

setup.art: A child sticking a red bindi on the top edge of a small hand mirror.
setup.caption: 1. Stick a bindi on the top edge of the hand mirror.

setup.art: A child standing about one step from a cupboard mirror, holding the hand mirror under her eyes, its face turned to the big mirror.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the hand mirror just under your eyes, facing the big mirror.

setup.art: The view in the big mirror: a tunnel of smaller and smaller hand mirrors, each with a red bindi, curving gently away into the dark.
setup.caption: 3. Look over the top. Count the bindis in the tunnel.

flow.do: 1. Stick a bindi on the top edge of the hand mirror, on the shiny side. 2. Stand your child about one step from the big mirror. 3. Ask the question below and write the guess.
flow.say: We're going to make a tunnel of mirrors. How many bindis do you think you'll see? 2, 10, 100, or more than anyone can count? Why?
flow.kid: How many bindis will you see? Why do you think so?

ask.q: How many bindis will you see? Why?
good: Lots, because mirrors copy each other.
Two, because there are two mirrors.
For ever, because it keeps going.

flow.context: This is the first step of the mirror tunnel. You set up and make your guess.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the hand mirror with both hands, just under the eyes. 2. The shiny side faces the big mirror. 3. Your child looks over the top edge into the big mirror. 4. Tilt the hand mirror a tiny bit until the tunnel appears. 5. Your child counts the bindis, three times.
flow.say: Look over the top of the little mirror, into the big one. Tilt it slowly. Can you see the tunnel? Count the bindis, starting with the biggest.
flow.kid: Look over the little mirror. Tilt it slowly. Count the bindis.
flow.parent: If no tunnel shows, keep the hand mirror upright and turn it a little left or right. The tunnel often curves gently away. Most people count between 6 and 15 before the copies get too small and dark.
flow.context: In this step of the mirror tunnel, you look and count.

flow.do: 1. Swap, and you count three times too. 2. Write all the counts in the table.
flow.say: Now it's my turn. Let's see if I count the same.
flow.kid: Now your grown-up counts. Write the numbers down.
flow.context: In this step of the mirror tunnel, the grown-up counts too.

flow.do: 1. Ask the questions below. 2. Then read the card on whether space goes on for ever.
flow.say: Could you count to the end? What did the last bindis look like? Was that really the end, or could you just not see more?
flow.kid: Could you see the end? What did the last bindis look like?

ask.q: Why could you not count any more bindis?
good: They got too small.
They got too dark.
They were too far down the tunnel.

check.q: In the mirror tunnel, what happened to the bindis as the tunnel went away?
check.why: Each copy is seen through more bounces, so its light has travelled farther, and far things look smaller. Each mirror also keeps a little of the light, so every copy is dimmer than the one before.

flow.parent: Each copy looks smaller because the light from it has travelled farther, just like the bottle from far away. A strong answer says the row faded out, and that you could not tell whether it really ended.
flow.context: This is the last step of the mirror tunnel. You talk about what you found.

activities.title: Space Hunt: find what is between things
activities.context: In this activity you hunt for spaces in your home: under, inside, around and between things. It is a way in before the bottle strip test.

materials.item: an empty plastic bottle with its cap

schedule.what: Find five spaces in the home. Push two tumblers together and look for the space around them.

activities.record: Draw or list five spaces you found.

setup.art: A child crouching to look at the space under a bed, and another arrow to the gap between her own spread fingers.
setup.caption: 1. Hunt for spaces: under, inside, around and between.

setup.art: Two steel tumblers pushed together on the floor, with a dotted line all around them.
setup.caption: 2. Push two tumblers together. Is there still space?

flow.do: 1. Put two tumblers on the floor, about one hand apart. 2. Point to the gap between them. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: What is between these two tumblers? Take a guess. What would you call it?
flow.kid: What is between the two tumblers?

good: Nothing.
Air.
Space.
A gap.

flow.parent: Every answer is fine for now. Introduce the word: the room between things is called space.
flow.context: This is the start of the space hunt.

flow.do: 1. Your child finds five spaces in the home. 2. Give hints if needed. Try between your fingers, under the bed and inside an empty bottle. 3. Also try between the fan blades, and between your child and the wall. 4. Write or draw each one.
flow.say: The room between things is called space. Let's hunt for five spaces. Look under, inside, around and between things.
flow.kid: Find five spaces. Look under, inside, around and between.
flow.parent: Keep fingers away from the fan blades. Look at the gaps only while the fan is switched off.

flow.do: 1. Push the two tumblers together until they touch. 2. Ask the questions below. 3. Close the empty bottle with its cap and squeeze it.
flow.say: Now the tumblers touch. Is there still space? Where? This bottle looks empty. Squeeze it with the cap on. What is inside?
flow.kid: The tumblers touch. Is there still space? Squeeze the shut bottle. What is inside?

good: All around the tumblers.
Inside them.
Above them, up to the ceiling.

ask.q: What is in the shut bottle?
good: Air. It pushes back when I squeeze.

flow.parent: The capped bottle pushes back because it is full of air. Space in a room is full of air, even where it looks empty.

activities.title: Step It Out: near, nearer, nearest
activities.context: In this activity you estimate how many steps it is to four places in your home. Then you walk and count. You put the places in order from nearest to farthest.

schedule.what: Guess the steps to four places, then walk heel to toe and count. Put the places in order.

activities.record: A table with each place, your guess and your count. Circle the nearest and the farthest.

setup.art: A child standing by her bed, pointing at the door, a window and the kitchen, with a thought bubble '8 steps?'.
setup.caption: 1. Guess how many steps to each place.

setup.art: Feet walking heel to toe across a floor, with numbers under each foot.
setup.caption: 2. Walk heel to toe and count.

flow.do: 1. Stand your child by the bed. 2. Choose four places: the door, a window, the kitchen and the cupboard. 3. Your child estimates the steps to each one. 4. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: How many steps from here to the door, do you think? And to the window? Make a careful guess. That is called an estimate.
flow.kid: Guess the steps to each place. That guess is an estimate.
flow.context: This is the start of Step It Out. You make your estimates.

flow.do: 1. Your child walks to each place heel to toe, counting out loud. 2. Write each count next to the guess.
flow.say: Now walk heel to toe, so every step is the same size. Count out loud.
flow.kid: Walk heel to toe. Count each step out loud.
flow.parent: Heel to toe keeps every step the same size, so the counts are fair to compare.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to put the four places in order, from nearest to farthest. 2. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Which place is nearest? Which is farthest? Were your guesses too big, too small, or close?
flow.kid: Which is nearest? Which is farthest? Were your guesses close?

ask.q: How do you know the kitchen is farther than the door?
good: It took more steps.
There is more space between me and the kitchen.

check.q: Farhan took 4 steps to the door and 9 steps to the kitchen. Which is nearer?
check.why: Fewer steps means less space between, so the door is nearer. 4 is less than 9.

activities.title: Draw Near and Far from the Window
activities.context: In this activity you look out of a window and draw what you see. You notice that far things look smaller, so artists draw them smaller and higher up the page.

schedule.what: Look out of the window. Draw one near thing and the same kind of thing far away.

activities.record: Your drawing, with 'near' and 'far' written by the two things.

setup.art: A window grille with a tree just outside and the same kind of tree tiny on a far hill or road.
setup.caption: 1. Find two of the same kind of thing, one near and one far.

setup.art: A child's drawing with a big tree at the bottom of the page and a small tree near the top.
setup.caption: 2. Draw them as big as they look.

flow.do: 1. Stand at a window with your child. 2. Find two of the same kind of thing: two trees, two buildings, two water tanks or two people.
flow.say: Can you find two of the same kind of thing, one near and one far? Which looks bigger?
flow.kid: Find two of the same thing, one near, one far.
flow.parent: If the window shows only one building, use a long corridor and two people, or two of the same shoes at different distances.
flow.context: This is the start of Draw Near and Far.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws the near thing and the far thing, each as big as it looks. 2. Then colours the drawing.
flow.say: Draw them just as big as they look, not as big as they really are.
flow.kid: Draw each one as big as it looks.

flow.do: 1. Ask the question below. 2. Write 'near' and 'far' by the two things.
flow.say: Is the far tree really that small? Why did you draw it small?
flow.kid: Is the far one really small? Why did you draw it small?

ask.q: Why did you draw the far one smaller?
good: It looks smaller because it is far away.
It is far, so it takes up less of what I see.

games.title: Nearer, Farther: find the hidden tumbler
games.context: This is a hiding game about near and far. One player hides a small steel tumbler. The others look for it, and the hider holds up cards to say nearer or farther.
rules: Cut out the five clue cards. Give them to the hider.
The seeker goes out of the room. The hider hides a small steel tumbler somewhere in the room.
The seeker comes back and starts to walk around.
The hider says nothing, and only holds up cards. 'Nearer' means you are getting closer. 'Farther' means you are moving away.
Hold up 'Very near' when the seeker is within one step, and 'Very far' when the seeker is on the other side of the room.
When the seeker finds the tumbler, hold up 'Found it!'. Count how many cards you showed. Then swap jobs.
The seeker who finds it with the fewest cards wins.

setup.art: A girl holding up a card that says 'Nearer' while her brother walks towards a cupboard.
setup.caption: 1. The hider holds up a card. The seeker walks.

setup.art: A small steel tumbler peeking out from behind a cushion, and the seeker reaching for it.
setup.caption: 2. Find the tumbler. Count the cards shown.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Read the rules out loud. 3. Agree on safe hiding places: no high shelves, nothing breakable.
flow.say: When you get closer, I'll hold up 'Nearer'. When you move away, 'Farther'. Use the cards to find the tumbler.
flow.kid: Watch the cards. Nearer means closer. Farther means moving away.
flow.context: This is the start of the hiding game.

flow.do: 1. Play at least four rounds, swapping hider and seeker. 2. Keep count of the cards shown each round.
flow.say: Nearer. Nearer. Oh, farther now. Very near!
flow.kid: Walk the way the cards tell you. Find the tumbler.

ask.q: What does 'nearer' tell you about the space between you and the tumbler?
good: It is getting smaller.
There is less space between us.

flow.do: 1. Count the cards for each round. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Which round was quickest? What helped you find it?
flow.kid: Which round was quickest? What helped?

check.q: In the hiding game, the hider holds up 'Farther'. What should the seeker do?
options: Turn and go back the other way
check.why: 'Farther' means the space between the seeker and the tumbler is growing. Going back the other way makes it shrink again.

games.title: Near to Far: a line-up card game
games.context: This is a card game about distance. Each card names a place. You line the cards up from nearest to you to farthest, then check the backs.

items.b: Nearest of all. It is on your own face.
Usually a short walk, a few minutes away.

items.f: A plane high in the sky
items.b: About 10 kilometres up. That is a walk of about 2 hours, if you could walk straight up.
About 400 kilometres up, in outer space. People live and work on board.

items.f: From the top of India to the bottom
items.b: About 3,200 kilometres, from Ladakh in the north to Kanyakumari in the south.
About 384,000 kilometres away. Light from the Moon takes just over 1 second to reach you.
About 150 million kilometres away. Its light takes about 8 minutes to reach you.

items.f: The nearest star after the Sun
items.b: So far that its light takes more than 4 years to reach us.
One of the farthest things you can see without a telescope, on a very dark night. Its light takes about 2.5 million years to reach us.

rules: Cut out the ten cards. Shuffle them.
Each player in turn takes a card and puts it in the line, where they think it goes: nearest at one end, farthest at the other.
A player may move one card that is already in the line, if they give a reason.
When all ten are in the line, turn them over and read the backs from nearest to farthest.
Count how many cards were in the right place. Shuffle and play again to beat your count.

setup.art: Ten cards laid in a line on the floor, from 'The tip of your nose' at one end to 'The Andromeda galaxy' at the other.
setup.caption: 1. Put the cards in a line, nearest to farthest.

setup.art: A child turning over the Moon card to read the back.
setup.caption: 2. Turn them over and check the backs.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards together. 2. Read the rules out loud. 3. Read each card's front out loud.
flow.say: Each card is a place. Let's put them in a line, from nearest to us to farthest away.
flow.kid: Put the places in a line. Nearest at this end. Farthest at that end.
flow.context: This is the start of the line-up game.

flow.do: 1. Take turns placing cards. 2. When the line is done, turn the cards over from the nearest end. 3. Read each back out loud.
flow.say: Where does the Moon go? Is the Moon nearer than the Sun, or farther? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Where does the Moon go? Is it nearer than the Sun?

ask.q: The Sun and the Moon look about the same size. How can you tell which is farther?
good: The Sun is much bigger, so it must be farther to look as small.
The back of the card says so.
The Moon can pass in front of the Sun.

flow.do: 1. Count the cards in the right place. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Which card surprised you most? Why?
flow.kid: Which card surprised you? Why?

check.q: Which of these is farthest from you?
check.why: A plane is about 10 kilometres up, the Moon about 384,000 kilometres away, and the Sun about 150 million kilometres away. The Sun is farthest by far.

projects.title: My Room Map: where things are and the space between
projects.context: In this project you draw a map of your room, the way a bird on the ceiling would see the room. On day 2 you add how many steps are between things.

materials.item: a sheet of paper with squares drawn on it, or squared maths paper

schedule.what: Draw your room from above: the walls, the door, the bed and two more things.
Count steps between things. Write the numbers on the map. Colour the empty floor.

projects.record: The finished map, with step numbers between things and the empty floor coloured in.

setup.art: A room seen from above, drawn on squared paper: a rectangle bed, a square cupboard, a door gap and a window.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your room from above, the way a bird on the ceiling would.

setup.art: The same map with arrows between the bed and the door marked '4 steps', and the empty floor coloured light blue.
setup.caption: 2. Add steps between things. Colour the empty space.

flow.do: 1. Stand at the door with your child. 2. Ask what the room would look like to a bird on the ceiling. 3. Your child draws the walls, the door, the bed and two more things on the squared paper.
flow.say: Imagine you are a bird on the ceiling, looking down. What shape is the bed from up there? Draw it.
flow.kid: Pretend you are a bird on the ceiling. Draw your room from above.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the room map.

flow.do: 1. Your child counts heel-to-toe steps between the bed and the door, and between two other things. 2. Writes the numbers on the map with arrows. 3. Colours all the empty floor.
flow.say: How many steps from the bed to the door? Write it on the map. Now colour all the empty floor. That is the space you can move in.
flow.kid: Count steps between things. Write them on the map. Colour the empty floor.

ask.q: Is there more space with things in it, or empty floor space?
good: More empty space.
More things. The bed is big.

flow.parent: Either answer is fine if your child can point to the evidence on the map.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the room map.
flow.wait: Do this on the next day.

challenges.title: Hide the Cupboard with a Coin
challenges.context: This is a puzzle challenge. A coin is far smaller than a cupboard. Can you make the coin hide the whole cupboard, without moving the cupboard?
challenges.problem: Make a small coin hide a whole cupboard from your view.
constraints: You may not move the cupboard.
You must hold the coin in your hand, at arm's length or nearer.
Close one eye when you look.
materials: a cupboard, a door or a tall fridge
paper and a pencil to write what you find
general: Stay where you are, and bring the coin nearer to your eye until it hides the cupboard.
Look out of a window. Hold the coin at arm's length, and find the far building, tree or water tank that it hides.
creative: Look through a rolled-up paper tube. Put the coin at the far end of the tube.
Try a bigger coin and a smaller one, and see which one you must hold nearer to your eye.
challenges.your_turn: Find your own way to make the coin hide the cupboard. Then try to hide something even bigger, like a building outside the window, with the coin.

setup.art: A child at arm's length holding a coin up in front of a cupboard, one eye closed, the coin covering only part of it.
setup.caption: 1. Hold up the coin. Does it hide the cupboard?

setup.art: The same child, now with the coin held close to her eye, and the coin covers the whole cupboard.
setup.caption: 2. Change the space between the coin and your eye, or between you and what you look at.

flow.do: 1. Explain the challenge. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: This coin is tiny, and the cupboard is huge. Can you make the coin hide the whole cupboard? You can't move the cupboard.
flow.kid: Can a small coin hide the whole cupboard? You can't move the cupboard.

good: Where I stand.
How near the coin is to my eye.

flow.do: 1. Your child tries ways to hide the cupboard. 2. Then your child looks out of a window and finds a far building that the coin hides.
flow.say: Try it. What do you need to change? Then try the coin on something far outside the window.
flow.kid: Try it. Then hide a far building with the coin.
flow.parent: Holding a coin close to the eye hides a lot at once. Walking back from a cupboard also works, but only in a very long hall, so the window is the easy second try.

flow.do: 1. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Did the coin get bigger, or the cupboard smaller? What really changed?
flow.kid: Did the coin grow? What changed?

check.q: How did the small coin hide the big cupboard?
options: The space between changed, so the cupboard looked smaller than the coin
check.why: Neither the coin nor the cupboard changed size. When the cupboard is far away, or the coin is very near your eye, the coin takes up more of what you see than the cupboard does.

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it means.
pairs: the room around things and between them
how much space there is between two things
items.why: These are the four words the child needs for this unit. Distance is a way of saying how much space is between things.

items.p: In the bottle strip test, the strip from 4 steps was shorter than the strip from 1 step. Why?
opts: You were farther away, so the bottle looked smaller
items.why: The bottle and the pencil stayed the same. Only the distance changed. Choosing 'the bottle got smaller' means thinking far things really shrink. Walking back and picking up the same bottle shows they do not.
items.context: This question is about the bottle strip test. You measured how tall a bottle looked from 1, 2 and 4 steps away.

items.p: Draw two of the same tree: one near you, and one far away.
items.a: A big tree low on the page and a small tree higher up.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the far tree smaller, because far things take up less of what we see. The trees are really the same size.
items.art: An empty box with 'near' at the bottom and 'far' at the top.

items.p: You are sitting on your bed. Sort these into 'near me' and 'far from me'.
items.why: Near things are a small distance away, like the pillow, toes and blanket. The plane, the Moon and the Sun are far, even though we can see them.

items.p: The space between your bed and the wall is completely empty, with nothing at all in it.
items.why: False. It is full of air. Air is made of tiny bits too small to see, but you feel them when you wave your hand fast.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: name two spaces you found in the space hunt.
items.a: For example: under the bed, and inside an empty bottle.
items.why: A strong answer names real spaces from the hunt, such as gaps between things or room inside things.

items.p: Ira, a girl in Class 2, counted 6 steps to the door and 3 steps to her bed. How many more steps is the door?
items.why: 6 take away 3 is 3. The door is 3 steps farther, so there is more space between Ira and the door.

items.p: Kavya and Meena are looking at the gap between a bed and a wall.

views.says: The gap is empty. There is nothing there.
The gap is not empty. It is full of air.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Meena, because a shut bottle pushes back when squeezed, so air fills space that looks empty. It also says Kavya is right that there are no things you can see in the gap.
items.why: Both have part of it. There are no toys or furniture in the gap, so it looks empty. But it is full of air. The squeezed bottle in the space hunt is the evidence.

items.p: Look at the picture of Revathi's room. Write 'near' or 'far' by each thing, for Revathi standing at the door.
labels: the window on the far wall
the shoe rack beside the door
a: the mat by her feet: near
the window on the far wall: far
the shoe rack beside the door: near
items.why: Things right by the door are a small distance from Revathi, so they are near. The window across the room is far.
items.art: A room drawn from the door, with a girl in the doorway, a mat at her feet, a shoe rack beside her and a window on the opposite wall.

items.p: Three of these are spaces. Which one is a thing, not a space?
items.why: The tumbler is a thing. It takes up space, and there is space all around it. The others are spaces between things or inside them.

items.p: In the mirror tunnel, how did each bindi look compared with the one before it?
items.why: The light from each copy travelled farther than the one before, so it looked smaller. Each mirror also keeps a little light, so it looked dimmer.
items.context: This question is about the mirror tunnel. You held a small mirror facing a big mirror and counted the copies of a bindi.

items.p: Put these in order, from nearest to you to farthest: the Moon, the ceiling fan, the Sun, a plane in the sky.
items.why: The fan is a few steps away, a plane about 10 kilometres up, the Moon about 384,000 kilometres away and the Sun about 150 million kilometres away.

items.p: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon. Why do they look about the same size in the sky?
items.a: The Sun is also about 400 times farther away, so it looks as small as the Moon.
items.why: A strong answer uses distance: far things look smaller. Saying 'the Sun is small' misses that the Sun is much bigger than the Moon.

items.p: In the bottle strip test, from twice as far away, the bottle looked about ________ as tall.
items.why: Twice the distance makes a thing look about half as tall. The folded strip showed this.
items.context: This question is about the bottle strip test. You measured how tall a bottle looked from 1, 2 and 4 steps away.

items.p: Draw your three strips from the bottle strip test, side by side, and write how many steps away each was.
items.a: Three strips getting shorter: 1 step longest, 2 steps about half, 4 steps shortest.
items.why: A strong drawing shows each strip shorter as the distance grows, with the 2-step strip about half the 1-step strip.
items.context: This question is about the bottle strip test. You measured how tall a bottle looked from 1, 2 and 4 steps away.
items.art: An empty box with three lines labelled '1 step', '2 steps', '4 steps'.

items.p: In the mirror tunnel, you could count the bindis all the way to the very end.
items.why: False. The copies got too small and dim to count. We could not tell whether the row really ended.
items.context: This question is about the mirror tunnel. You held a small mirror facing a big mirror and counted the copies of a bindi.

items.p: Gauri and Zoya are talking about space.

views.says: Space must end somewhere. Everything has an end, like a road or a rope.
Space can't end. If there were a wall at the end, there would be more space on the other side.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: Any side, with a reason. A strong answer says that nobody knows yet, and uses something from the unit, such as the mirror tunnel or the stick question of Archytas.
items.why: This is a real open question. Gauri is right that most things we know have an end. Zoya uses the same idea Archytas used. Scientists still disagree, so a strong answer gives a reason, not only a side.

items.p: Bornali's strip from 1 step was 8 centimetres long. About how long was her strip from 2 steps?
items.why: Twice as far makes the bottle look about half as tall. Half of 8 is 4.
items.context: This question is about the bottle strip test. You measured how tall a bottle looked from 1, 2 and 4 steps away.

items.p: Two lamp posts on a road are the same height. One looks big and one looks small. Label which is near and which is far.
items.why: The posts are the same height, so the one that looks smaller must be farther away.
items.art: A road going away, with a tall lamp post in front and a small-looking one far down the road.

items.p: Tsering, a girl in Leh, sees two mountains that look the same height. One is much farther away. What can she say?
opts: The farther one is really taller
The nearer one is really taller
items.why: Far things look smaller. If the far mountain looks as tall as the near one, it must really be taller. This is how the Sun can be much bigger than the Moon but look the same.

items.p: Your thumb can hide a whole building. Is your thumb bigger than the building? Explain.
items.a: No. The building is much bigger, but it is far away, so it looks smaller than my thumb near my eye.
items.why: A strong answer says the building only looks small because of the distance, and that the thumb is very near the eye.

items.p: Nila stands 10 steps from a lamp post. She walks back until the post looks half as tall. About how far is she now?
items.why: Twice as far makes a thing look half as tall. Twice 10 is 20. Choosing 5 steps would mean walking nearer, which makes things look bigger.

items.p: Sneha and her brother Arjun are arguing about space.

views.says: Space is like a huge empty box. Even with nothing in it, the space would still be there.
Space is only the gaps between things. With no things at all, there would be no space.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: Any side, with a reason. A strong answer notices that we always measure space using things, like steps between the bed and the door.
items.why: This is a real argument. Isaac Newton thought like Sneha. Gottfried Leibniz thought like Arjun. Thinkers still argue about it.

items.p: Draw what you think is at the edge of space, if there is an edge. Then write one question about your drawing.
items.a: Any drawing, with a question such as 'What is past the wall?'
items.why: A strong answer shows an idea and asks what is beyond it, the way Archytas did. Nobody knows the answer.
items.art: An empty box with stars at one side.

items.p: Sort these into 'scientists know this' and 'nobody knows yet'.
items: The Sun is farther away than the Moon
Whether space goes on for ever
What is past the farthest place we can see
items.why: Distances to the Sun and Moon, and how empty space is, have been measured. Whether space ends, and what is beyond what we can see, are still unknown.

items.p: Out between the stars, space holds as much air as your room.
items.why: False. Between the stars, space is almost empty. A space the size of a sugar cube holds about one tiny bit of gas, while your room's air is crowded with them.

items.p: Three of these look small because they are far away. Which one looks small because it really is small?
opts: A plane high in the sky
items.why: The ant is right on your hand, so she is near, and she is really small. The star, the plane and the Moon are very big and very far away.

items.p: Put these in order, from the shortest time for their light to reach us to the longest: the Sun, the Moon, the nearest star after the Sun.
items: the nearest star after the Sun
items.why: Moonlight takes just over 1 second, sunlight about 8 minutes, and light from the nearest other star more than 4 years. The farther away, the longer light takes.

items.p: Look at the picture of the mirror tunnel. Label the copy whose light travelled the shortest way, and the copy whose light travelled the longest way.
labels: the smallest copy you can see
a: the smallest copy you can see: longest way
items.why: Each copy is seen after more bounces, so its light travels farther. Farther away looks smaller, so the smallest copy's light came the longest way.
items.context: This question is about the mirror tunnel. You held a small mirror facing a big mirror and counted the copies of a bindi.
items.art: A tunnel of hand mirrors getting smaller, each with a bindi, with two empty label boxes, one by the biggest and one by the smallest.

items.p: If the Sun were moved twice as far away, it would look about ________ as wide as it does now.
items.why: Twice as far makes a thing look about half as big, as in the bottle strip test. The Sun itself would not change.

opts: The room around things and between them
Only places with nothing in them
quiz.why: Space is everywhere, not only in the sky. It is the room around and between all things, even between your nose and this page.

quiz.p: Which of these is nearest to you right now?
quiz.why: Your nose is on your face, so there is almost no space between it and you. The door is a few steps away, and the Moon is very far.

quiz.p: Lakshmi counted 5 steps to the window and 9 steps to the door. Which is farther from her?
quiz.why: More steps means more space between, so the door is farther. 9 is more than 5.

quiz.p: Meenakshi looks at a bottle from 2 steps, then from 4 steps. How does it look from 4 steps?
quiz.why: From farther away, the bottle takes up less of what she sees, so it looks smaller. The bottle itself does not change.

quiz.p: A thing that is far away is really smaller than the same thing close up.
quiz.why: False. It only looks smaller. Walk up to it, and you find it is the same size as before.

quiz.p: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon. Why does it look about the same size?
opts: It is also about 400 times farther away
It is nearer than the Moon
quiz.why: Far things look smaller. The Sun is much bigger, and also much farther away, so in the sky they look about the same.

quiz.p: A plane high in the sky looks as small as a bird. Why?
opts: The plane shrinks when it flies
quiz.why: A plane is about 10 kilometres up. It is very big, but from so far away it takes up only a tiny part of what you see.

quiz.p: Does space go on for ever?
opts: No, there is a wall at the end
quiz.why: Nobody knows. We can only see part of space, and scientists still disagree. Thinking 'there is a wall' leads to the next question: what is on the other side?

quiz.p: In the mirror tunnel, why could you not see the end of the row?
opts: The copies got too small and dim to see
There was a wall at the end
quiz.why: Each copy was farther and dimmer than the one before, until you could not see them any more. That did not show whether the row ended.

quiz.p: What fills the space in your room between the bed and the wall?
quiz.why: The space looks empty, but it is full of air. A shut bottle pushes back when you squeeze it, because it is full of air.

quiz.p: What is outer space like, out between the stars?
opts: Full of air, like your room
quiz.why: Out between the stars, there is only about one tiny bit of gas in a space the size of a sugar cube. It is almost empty.

applications: Artists draw far things smaller and higher on the page, so a flat drawing looks deep. This is called perspective.
Drivers and cyclists judge how much space there is before they turn, so they do not bump into things.

Scientists at ISRO, including Ritu Karidhal and Nandini Harinath, worked on Mangalyaan, India's spacecraft that reached Mars in 2014. Getting there meant working out a path across a huge distance of space.
Phone maps measure the distance between two places and tell us how long a journey will take.
Astronomers use Henrietta Leavitt's rule to measure how far away other galaxies are.

open_questions.q: Does space go on for ever, or does it have an end?
open_questions.why_open: We can only see part of space, because light from farther away has not reached us yet. Measurements of the shape of space fit space going on for ever, but they also fit space being very big and curving round. Nobody knows yet.

open_questions.q: Is space a thing of its own, or only the gaps between things?
open_questions.why_open: Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz argued about this over 300 years ago. Later, scientists found that space can bend and stretch, which you will learn about later. Thinkers still disagree about what space really is.

open_questions.q: What is past the farthest galaxies we can see?
open_questions.why_open: Telescopes keep finding galaxies farther and farther away. But light from beyond a certain distance has not had time to reach us, so we cannot see what is there.

maths.problem: In Step It Out, Lakshmi estimated 10 steps to the kitchen. When she walked and counted, it was 7 steps. Was her estimate too big or too small, and by how many steps?
maths.explain: 10 is more than 7, so the estimate was too big. 10 take away 7 is 3.
maths.context: This question is about Step It Out. You guessed how many steps to places in your home, then walked and counted.
maths.why_maths: Comparing an estimate with a count shows how good our guesses about distance are, and helps us guess better next time.

maths.problem: In the bottle strip test, Ananya's strip from 1 step was 12 centimetres long. Her strip from 2 steps was 6 centimetres. She folds the 12 centimetre strip in half. How long is each half? What does that show?
maths.answer: Each half is 6 centimetres. That shows the bottle looked half as tall from twice as far away.
maths.explain: Half of 12 is 6. The folded half is as long as the 2-step strip, so from 2 steps the bottle looked half as tall.
maths.context: This question is about the bottle strip test. You measured how tall a bottle looked from 1, 2 and 4 steps away.
maths.why_maths: Folding in half lets you check 'half as tall' with your own hands, without a ruler.

maths.problem: Ananya's strips were 12 centimetres from 1 step, 6 centimetres from 2 steps and 3 centimetres from 4 steps. Spot the pattern. About how long would her strip be from 8 steps?
maths.explain: Each time the steps double, the strip is half as long: 12, 6, 3. Half of 3 is 1 and a half.
maths.context: This question is about the bottle strip test. You measured how tall a bottle looked from 1, 2 and 4 steps away.
maths.why_maths: A pattern lets you predict a result you have not measured, then test it.

maths.problem: On Revathi's room map, the bed is 2 squares from the door, and the cupboard is 5 squares from the door. Which is nearer the door, and by how many squares?
maths.explain: 2 is less than 5, so the bed is nearer. 5 take away 2 is 3.
maths.context: This question is about the room map. You drew your room from above on squared paper.
maths.why_maths: Squares on a map show distance, so you can compare how near things are just by counting.

roots.context: We have hunted for spaces, counted steps, measured a bottle from near and far, and looked into a tunnel of mirrors. Now we ask what space tells us about the world, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Your bottle stayed the same size all through the test. Yet from twice as far away, it looked about half as tall. Only the space between you and the bottle had changed. So you cannot tell how big a thing is just by looking, unless you know how far away it is.
deep_truth.habit: We take how big a thing looks to be how big it is. The bottle test shows that the size we see depends on the space between us and the thing. That is how the Sun, about 400 times wider than the Moon, can look the same size.
deep_truth.evidence: In the bottle strip test, the 2-step strip was about half the 1-step strip, and the bottle never moved or changed.

three.who_am_i: You take up a little space, and there is space all around you. Wherever you go, you are somewhere, near some things and far from others.
three.what_is_life: Living beings need space: room for a seed's roots to spread, for a bird on a wire, for a child to run. A plant in a crowded pot grows poorly.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is things with space between them, from the gap under your bed to the huge distances between the stars. Nobody knows yet whether that space ever ends.

roots.thread: Space is what lets things be apart, so that there can be near and far. The bottle looked small only because of the space between you and it. Everything is conscious, the bottle and the stars too, each meeting the world in their own way. Many scientists disagree, and say only living beings with brains are aware.

teachings.teaching: Thirty spokes meet at the hub of a wheel, and the empty centre makes the wheel useful. A clay pot is useful because of the empty space inside. Doors and windows are useful because they are openings.
teachings.link: In the space hunt, the empty space inside the bottle and the tiffin box is what makes them useful. Space between things is not nothing. It is what lets us use and move things.

teachings.source: Jain thought, the Tattvartha Sutra, chapter 5
teachings.teaching: Jain thinkers taught that space, called akasha, gives room to everything. They said the part of space where things live has an edge, and that beyond it lies empty space that goes on without end.
teachings.link: Jain thinkers asked the same question as the mirror tunnel: does space go on for ever? Their answer was that the world has an edge, but space itself does not.

teachings.teaching: The hymn asks how the world began, and ends by asking whether anyone really knows, perhaps not even the one who watches from the highest heaven.
teachings.link: Scientists today still cannot say whether space goes on for ever. Saying honestly 'nobody knows yet' is part of science.

science.text: From twice as far away, a thing looks about half as tall. This is why the Sun, about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away, looks the same size.
Outer space between the stars is almost empty, with about one tiny bit of gas in a space the size of a sugar cube.
Measurements of the shape of space fit space going on for ever, but they also fit space being very big and curving round on itself. Nobody knows which is true.

other_view.who: Aristotle, a thinker in ancient Greece, about 2,350 years ago
other_view.view: Aristotle taught that there can be no truly empty space anywhere, and that the world is a ball with an edge, with nothing at all beyond it. Many people today also say that bottles, stars and space have no awareness at all.

Mean distances: Moon about 384,400 km, Sun about 149.6 million km. Diameters: Moon about 3,474 km, Sun about 1,391,000 km. So the Sun is about 400 times wider and about 390 times farther away.
Light travel times: Moon about 1.3 seconds, Sun about 8 minutes 20 seconds, Proxima Centauri about 4.2 years, Andromeda galaxy about 2.5 million years.
Interstellar medium: an average density of roughly one atom per cubic centimetre, much less in many regions.
Planck Collaboration, 2018 results: space is measured to be flat to within about 0.2 percent, which fits an infinite universe or a very large finite one.

playtest: Thought through as a parent and child in a flat. The bottle strip test needs about 3 metres in a straight line, which most halls or bedroom-to-wall spaces give. With a half-litre bottle and a child's arm of about 45 cm, the marks come out roughly 12 to 14 cm from 1 big step, 6 to 7 cm from 2 steps and 3 to 4 cm from 4 steps, so the halving is easy to see by folding. Children of 7 often bend the arm, so the grown-up checks it, or measures with their own arm while the child checks. The mirror tunnel needs a wall or cupboard mirror and a hand mirror, found in most homes. Most people count 6 to 15 copies before they fade. The space hunt and Step It Out need nothing special. The coin challenge works best by holding the coin close to the eye, since few flats are long enough to walk back far.
